blocks.title: Exact excerpt — systems_examples/ch01/main.cpp:8–12
Read each source line
items: Line 8: const makes total read-only after initialization. int is the whole-number type. The + expression adds 7 and 5 at execution; = initializes the named result to 12. The compiler checks the types and may precompute this constant expression.
Line 9: std:: names the standard-library namespace. ostringstream is an output stream that collects formatted text in an owned string rather than writing it immediately to a terminal.
Line 10: For streams, << inserts the value on its right into the stream on its left. The quoted label is text; total supplies the number to format.
Line 11: message.str() returns the collected text. std::cout sends it to standard output, and the character literal \n supplies a newline. The operating system handles the underlying output service.
Line 12: assert checks a Boolean condition during this verification build and stops the program if it is false. It does not prove the program correct for inputs the test never tried.

topics.summary: A value parameter creates a separate vector object. A reference parameter, marked &, names the existing vector. The empty check is a precondition check performed before indexing; throwing leaves the original vector unchanged. Return-by-value lets the returned vector own its storage without a dangling reference.

blocks.title: Exact excerpt — systems_examples/ch02/main.cpp:7–11
Read each source line
items: Line 7: auto asks the compiler to infer the type. No & appears, so copy is a separate vector with separate element storage.

Line 11: The colon in this range-based for means take each element from readings in order. const int value makes a read-only value copy for that iteration; it is not a reference because there is no &. The stream prints each value followed by a space.

topics.title: Exercise 4: Choose a design
topics.summary: What extra check is needed if field comes from user input? Compare the selected design with this plausible alternative: Separate integer members are simpler when compact storage or a device format is not required.

blocks.title: Hint — open after your first attempt
blocks.text: Name the expected change or workload first. Compare guarantees, ownership, and the cost of added machinery.

blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text: Reject values above 15, or explicitly define truncation with field & 0xF. Silently spilling into nearby fields would violate the preservation requirement. The extended lab uses this reasoning: The setter clears the old four-bit field before inserting the new one. The two groups do not overlap, so bitwise OR combines them without carrying. Unsigned operations avoid sign-extension questions. The check belongs inside the setter because every caller must obey the same width rule. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

topics.title: Exercise 4: Choose a design
topics.summary: What replaces 100 when checking the representable range of std::size_t? Compare the selected design with this plausible alternative: A fixed-size array avoids dynamic byte-count arithmetic when the bound is small and known.

blocks.title: Hint — open after your first attempt
blocks.text: Name the expected change or workload first. Compare guarantees, ownership, and the cost of added machinery.

blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text: Use std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max(), then separately compare with any allocation or application limit. Arithmetic safety does not guarantee allocation success. The extended lab uses this reasoning: The check divides before multiplying, so the product is formed only when it is within the caller’s limit. optional distinguishes a successful zero from rejection. A checked byte count still does not promise memory is available: allocation failure is a separate boundary. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

topics.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
topics.summary: An absolute tolerance gives a useful bound near zero; a relative tolerance scales with magnitude. The application chooses both from its error budget. Closeness is not a universal equivalence relation: it can fail transitivity, so it must not replace ordering in a sorted container. This lab covers modest finite magnitudes; a fully general comparator must also avoid overflow in difference and tolerance calculations.

topics.title: Exercise 4: Choose a design
topics.summary: Can this bump model release the first allocation while keeping the second and recover that hole? Compare the selected design with this plausible alternative: Use normal containers or a standard allocator unless measured allocation costs or a shared lifetime justify a custom arena.

blocks.title: Hint — open after your first attempt
blocks.text: Name the expected change or workload first. Compare guarantees, ownership, and the cost of added machinery.

blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text: Not with just the used counter. It supports simple allocation and whole-arena reset. General freeing needs extra state, such as a free list, and different guarantees. The extended lab uses this reasoning: Padding is computed separately and checked against remaining space before addition. The state changes only after every bound passes, which makes failure leave the arena usable. Returning an optional offset distinguishes rejection from a valid start at zero. This bump model has no individual free operation and does not create C++ objects in raw storage. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

topics.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
topics.summary: The guard avoids computing source.size()+1, which could overflow at the type boundary. The caller must supply a live writable range of capacity bytes when capacity is nonzero. A check on a number cannot prove an arbitrary pointer is valid. An owned string is simpler when the external interface does not require a caller-owned buffer.

discussion.question: An implementation makes this mistake: Accept source.size() <= capacity. An exactly full source then writes its null terminator one byte past the destination. Explain the failure and repair it. Identify one check that would expose the mistake.
discussion.hint: Find the rule that must hold before the operation touches data or commits state.
discussion.answer: Require source.size() < capacity and test the exact-fit boundary including the terminator. Relevant checks: cat needs capacity four including its trailing null. topics.title: Exercise 4: Choose a design
topics.summary: Is catching every bounds exception enough to make a parser correct? Compare the selected design with this plausible alternative: A range-based loop is less error-prone when every element should be visited.

blocks.title: Hint — open after your first attempt
blocks.text: Name the expected change or workload first. Compare guarantees, ownership, and the cost of added machinery.

blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text: No. Validate the expected format and length before using indexes. Exceptions catch this symptom, but the parser must still define what incomplete input means. The extended lab uses this reasoning: The guard avoids computing source.size()+1, which could overflow at the type boundary. The caller must supply a live writable range of capacity bytes when capacity is nonzero. A check on a number cannot prove an arbitrary pointer is valid. An owned string is simpler when the external interface does not require a caller-owned buffer. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

reading.title: Where the simple approach fails
paragraphs: Applying the EAX clearing rule to AX leads to an incorrect trace. Width is part of the instruction’s meaning.

topics.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
topics.summary: The write width is part of the operation, so the function receives it explicitly instead of guessing from the numeric value. Masking the new low bits prevents them from affecting preserved bits. Rejecting widths the model does not implement is more honest than silently applying a different rule. This models ISA behavior; it does not force the compiler to use a specific register.

items: Line 8: Converting the unsigned 32-bit value 7 to 64 bits gives 7 with zero high bits. This models the high-half clearing caused by an x86 EAX write.

discussion.answer: It can use proven facts about aliasing, control flow, and the language rules. It must preserve observable behavior for all defined inputs, not just one test. The extended lab uses this reasoning: A const reference prevents mutation through that reference; it does not prove the underlying object cannot change through another name. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

reading.title: Where the simple approach fails
paragraphs: Checking only in user code is insufficient when a privileged service receives requests from untrusted callers.
A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Check offset+length <= extent without checking overflow. A very large length can wrap the sum.

topics.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
topics.summary: The model separates permission from presence. Missing backing is recoverable only when the mapping policy allows the access. The instruction advances after success, preserving the restart point across a repair. This is a model of architectural control transfer, not a real exception handler or a promise that every page fault is repaired.

discussion.question: Could a denied write be part of normal copy-on-write behavior?

topics.title: Exercise 4: Choose a design
topics.summary: Why is a valid bit also needed even when the stored tag equals zero? Compare the selected design with this plausible alternative: More ways per set permit several competing tags, but require a choice when the set fills.

blocks.title: Hint — open after your first attempt
blocks.text: Name the expected change or workload first. Compare guarantees, ownership, and the cost of added machinery.

blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text: A cold, unused entry can contain an arbitrary or zero tag. The valid bit says whether the entry actually represents cached data. The extended lab uses this reasoning: Division removes the byte offset, modulo selects a set, and the remaining quotient distinguishes competing blocks. Powers of two allow bit-field extraction, but this numeric model also supports other positive sizes. Decomposition does not test whether the cache line is valid or resident; lookup needs that additional state. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

topics.summary: Calling the second access to block 0 a compulsory miss is wrong. That block has been seen before; this eviction is a conflict relative to a four-line fully associative LRU reference.

reading.title: Where the simple approach fails
paragraphs: Calling the second access to block 0 a compulsory miss is wrong. That block has been seen before; this eviction is a conflict relative to a four-line fully associative LRU reference.
A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Initialize unsigned slots to zero and compare only the stored value. The first access to block zero is incorrectly called a hit.
The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Represent validity explicitly, with optional or a valid bit, and include block zero as the first cold access in a test.

topics.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
topics.summary: optional gives each slot an empty state separate from every unsigned block number, including zero. The vector is local to the simulation call, so repeated tests start cold rather than sharing hidden history. On a miss, the selected slot is replaced; the other slots keep their state. The function reports events, not elapsed time.

reading.title: Execution trace and checked output
paragraphs: A cold direct-mapped cache has four lines of 16 bytes. Read addresses 0, 16, 0, 64, 0, 16. Predict the output before running the complete example.

Read 0, 16, 0: miss, miss, hit The first two reads bring in blocks 0 and 1; the third reuses block 0. Read 64, 0: miss, miss Block 4 replaces block 0 in slot 0; returning to 0 must fetch it again. Read 16: hit; total 2 hits out of 6 Slot 1 still contains block 1. Hit rate is 2/6, about 33.3%.

blocks.title: Exact excerpt — systems_examples/ch30/main.cpp:11–14
Read each source line
items: Line 11: The slot holds a complete block number in this small model. Equality means the requested block is already resident; -1 represents an empty slot.
Line 12: Adding a Boolean adds one for true and zero for false. hits records observed hits before any replacement.
Line 13: Install the requested block even on a miss. This can evict another block mapped to the same slot.
Line 14: Print H for the previously observed hit, M otherwise. Testing after installation would falsely turn every access into a hit.

discussion.hint: Use one successful case, one rejected or boundary case, and one ownership or state rule. A claim about speed requires measurements, not just a diagram.
discussion.answer: The slice owns its returned characters, so it does not depend on the original string’s later lifetime. The checks use the valid input extent, not its allocation capacity. An optional empty string is a success, while an empty optional is rejection. Real file reads can also fail or return fewer bytes; this memory model isolates the bounds contract. The maintenance decision follows from this repair: Represent the success state separately from its data. Test the boundary at exactly end and just beyond end.

topics.title: Exercise 4: Choose a design
topics.summary: Would unmapping the private view make its changes appear in the file? Compare the selected design with this plausible alternative: Explicit read/write calls can be clearer for streaming access; mapping can suit random access when lifetime and bounds are controlled.

blocks.title: Hint — open after your first attempt
blocks.text: Name the expected change or workload first. Compare guarantees, ownership, and the cost of added machinery.

blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text: No. A private mapping does not promise to write its modifications back as shared file changes. Use the correct mapping or explicit write path for that requirement. The extended lab uses this reasoning: Shared ownership and shared data are related but different facts. A shared_ptr keeps this object alive; a separate string snapshot copies its characters. A real memory mapping is governed by OS mapping and file-lifetime rules rather than shared_ptr counts. The model makes the intended aliasing and cleanup relationships inspectable without pretending to implement mmap. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

topics.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
topics.summary: The handle is not the open-file description. Each process can close its own inherited descriptor while the kernel object remains referenced by another descriptor. The description holds the shared offset in this model. These smart pointers exist in one C++ process and illustrate the relationship; they are not the implementation of fork.

discussion.question: Why can buffered text be printed twice if buffered output exists before fork?

topics.title: Exercise 4: Choose a design
topics.summary: What should happen for the incomplete input emit | ? Compare the selected design with this plausible alternative: For a fixed external command, a direct argument-vector API is safer and simpler than invoking a shell parser.

blocks.title: Hint — open after your first attempt
blocks.text: Name the expected change or workload first. Compare guarantees, ownership, and the cost of added machinery.

blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text: Reject it as a syntax error before launching emit. Starting part of an invalid pipeline creates side effects and cleanup work without a complete execution plan. The extended lab uses this reasoning: Parsing produces an execution plan before any process is launched. The result owns its stage names, so it survives destruction of the input stream. Rejecting unsupported forms makes the small grammar explicit; it would be incorrect to advertise this whitespace parser as a general shell parser. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

blocks.title: Exact excerpt — systems_examples/ch43/main.cpp:6–9
Read each source line
items: Line 6: A takes a snapshot of counter while it is zero. This whole program is single-threaded so the illustrated interleaving is fully defined.
Line 7: B takes its snapshot before either modeled write, also seeing zero.
Line 8: A writes its old snapshot plus one, giving counter 1.

Line 9: B writes its own old snapshot plus one, again 1. The second store replaces the first update. Real unsynchronized ordinary C++ thread writes would have undefined behavior, not a guaranteed result of 1.

reading.title: Failure diagnosis and repair
paragraphs: In pop, return no value whenever closed_ is true, even if items_ is nonempty. Buffered work is lost during shutdown.
After waiting, return no value only when the queue is empty. A closed queue can still contain items that the drain contract promises to deliver.

The reference solution makes the contract executable with assertions. A class is useful here because the mutex, predicates, queue, capacity, and closed flag must obey one shared rule across several operations. All shared state is accessed under the mutex. Separate conditions describe available items and available space. The producer closes on normal completion and on exceptions so the consumer cannot wait forever for more input. The queue must outlive every participant.

topics.summary: If shutdown occurs with two queued items, should consumers drop them? Compare the selected design with this plausible alternative: An unbounded queue simplifies insertion but can turn overload into unbounded memory use.

blocks.title: Hint — open after your first attempt
blocks.text: Name the expected change or workload first. Compare guarantees, ownership, and the cost of added machinery.

blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text: Either draining or discarding can be valid, but the contract must choose. A drainable queue rejects new pushes and lets consumers finish existing items before reporting closed-and-empty. The extended lab uses this reasoning: A class is useful here because the mutex, predicates, queue, capacity, and closed flag must obey one shared rule across several operations. All shared state is accessed under the mutex. Separate conditions describe available items and available space. The producer closes on normal completion and on exceptions so the consumer cannot wait forever for more input. The queue must outlive every participant. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

reading.title: Where the simple approach fails
paragraphs: Ordering only some call sites is insufficient. Other locks, callbacks, or blocking operations can introduce different cycles.
A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Lock the source mutex first and destination second in both transfer directions. Each thread can hold the lock the other needs.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Use a consistent global ordering or an appropriate multi-mutex acquisition operation. Separately handle repeated references to the same resource.

blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text:
Expected output:
3,8 3,8

Forward transfer: request 3 then 8. A globally consistent order prevents one participant from taking the opposite order.
Reverse transfer: still request 3 then 8. Business direction is separated from lock acquisition order.
Rule out this cycle: no participant holds 8 while waiting for 3 under this rule. The rule removes circular waiting among locks covered by the same total order.

topics.title: Exercise 4: Choose a design
topics.summary: What if the transfer is from an account to itself? Compare the selected design with this plausible alternative: std::scoped_lock can acquire multiple distinct mutexes with deadlock avoidance; a single mutex is simpler if contention is acceptable.

blocks.title: Hint — open after your first attempt
blocks.text: Name the expected change or workload first. Compare guarantees, ownership, and the cost of added machinery.

blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text: Handle that case explicitly. Attempting to lock the same non-recursive mutex twice can deadlock or violate a locking API’s requirements. The extended lab uses this reasoning: scoped_lock acquires the two distinct mutexes using a deadlock-avoidance strategy and releases both at scope exit. Handling the same-account case first avoids passing the same non-recursive mutex twice. The small fixed total bounds arithmetic in this fixture. Other locks, callbacks, or I/O added inside the critical section would introduce new waiting relationships that still need review. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

topics.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
topics.summary: A byte stream can split or combine application frames arbitrarily. The parser therefore returns both owned payload data and a consumed count. It does not erase unconsumed bytes itself. Bounds are checked before forming payload iterators, and invalid size is distinct from incomplete arrival. Network errors and end-of-stream handling belong to the surrounding connection state machine.

topics.title: Exercise 4: Choose a design
topics.summary: What should happen if the peer claims a million-byte frame but the service limit is 8? Compare the selected design with this plausible alternative: A delimiter can be simpler for text, provided escaping and maximum line length are defined.

blocks.title: Hint — open after your first attempt
blocks.text: Name the expected change or workload first. Compare guarantees, ownership, and the cost of added machinery.

blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text: Reject the length before allocating or waiting for that payload. Framing includes resource limits as well as byte boundaries. The extended lab uses this reasoning: A byte stream can split or combine application frames arbitrarily. The parser therefore returns both owned payload data and a consumed count. It does not erase unconsumed bytes itself. Bounds are checked before forming payload iterators, and invalid size is distinct from incomplete arrival. Network errors and end-of-stream handling belong to the surrounding connection state machine. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

discussion.answer:
Would-block means the operation cannot make immediate progress; EOF means the stream has ended. Keeping them separate prevents a temporary lack of data from closing a connection. The model gives -1 one special meaning, while a real read returning -1 requires inspecting errno. The fixture uses small counts; production accumulation also needs an explicit buffer-size bound. Full reference source: systems_labs/ch53/solution.cpp.
Expected solution output:
blocked-bytes=3 eof-bytes=2

topics.summary: Why should hardened builds still validate input lengths? Compare the selected design with this plausible alternative: Use layered platform mitigations alongside safe interfaces and verification, and inspect the actual build settings rather than assuming flags took effect.

blocks.title: Hint — open after your first attempt
blocks.text: Name the expected change or workload first. Compare guarantees, ownership, and the cost of added machinery.

blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text: Mitigations reduce some consequences or detect some faults; they do not make an invalid access correct. Preventing the out-of-bounds operation remains the primary rule. The extended lab uses this reasoning: A check proves only the fact it actually checks. This guard comparison can notice a changed guard value; it does not validate payload semantics or enforce bounds. The deliberate assignments are legal C++ operations, so the demonstration does not rely on undefined overflow behavior. Real mitigations add distinct defenses but do not replace a correct memory-access contract. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

topics.title: Exercise 4: Choose a design
topics.summary: Does an atomic rename alone guarantee data survives a power failure? Compare the selected design with this plausible alternative: A memory-only swap is sufficient for process-local state; durable external state requires a documented failure model.

blocks.title: Hint — open after your first attempt
blocks.text: Name the expected change or workload first. Compare guarantees, ownership, and the cost of added machinery.

blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text: No. Atomic visibility and crash durability are different contracts. A real protocol needs the relevant file and directory synchronization rules for its filesystem and OS. The extended lab uses this reasoning: from_chars reports both an error and the point where parsing stopped, so accepting a numeric prefix alone is not enough. The candidate must fit the entire grammar and range. A separately built string provides a commit point through swap; invalid input leaves the old value untouched. This is process-local exception-safe state replacement, not a durable file transaction. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

reading.title: Where the simple approach fails
paragraphs: This fixed six-element teaching program does not handle arbitrary sizes, worker-start failure recovery, or cancellation. Those are explicit extension tasks, not implied guarantees.

A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Let workers push_back into the shared results vector without a lock, or let main return before collecting workers. The first can race on container internals; the second can leave dangling references.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Allocate the result slots before starting workers, assign each slot to one input, and keep all shared objects alive through worker completion. Preserve close-and-collect cleanup if any operation fails.

topics.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
topics.summary: Work items own their strings, so queue operations do not leave borrowed input pointers behind. Main assigns each index once; workers therefore write distinct result elements without resizing the vector. Queue predicates and close are protected by one mutex. Every normal and exceptional path closes the queue and collects workers before local shared state dies. Main prints after collection, so scheduling does not reorder the report. Queue capacity bounds queued jobs; it does not bound the already-loaded input vector’s total memory. A streaming input layer would need its own size and backpressure contract.

discussion.question: Which change is needed first to support seven inputs with two workers? Compare the selected design with this plausible alternative: Start with a sequential reference and a clear input contract. Parallelize only after measurements show enough work to justify the coordination.
discussion.hint: Name the expected change or workload first. Compare guarantees, ownership, and the cost of added machinery.
discussion.answer: Compute ranges from size and worker count instead of hardcoding groups of three, then test that ranges cover every index once. Preserve lifetime and disjoint result ownership while changing the partition rule. The extended lab uses this reasoning: Work items own their strings, so queue operations do not leave borrowed input pointers behind. Main assigns each index once; workers therefore write distinct result elements without resizing the vector. Queue predicates and close are protected by one mutex. Every normal and exceptional path closes the queue and collects workers before local shared state dies. Main prints after collection, so scheduling does not reorder the report. Queue capacity bounds queued jobs; it does not bound the already-loaded input vector’s total memory. A streaming input layer would need its own size and backpressure contract. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

blocks.title: Hint — open after your first attempt
blocks.text: Use one successful case, one rejected or boundary case, and one ownership or state rule. A claim about speed requires measurements, not just a diagram.

blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text: Work items own their strings, so queue operations do not leave borrowed input pointers behind. Main assigns each index once; workers therefore write distinct result elements without resizing the vector. Queue predicates and close are protected by one mutex. Queue capacity bounds queued jobs; it does not bound the already-loaded input vector’s total memory. A streaming input layer would need its own size and backpressure contract. The maintenance decision follows from this repair: Allocate the result slots before starting workers, assign each slot to one input, and keep all shared objects alive through worker completion. Preserve close-and-collect cleanup if any operation fails.

paragraphs: Work items own their strings, so queue operations do not leave borrowed input pointers behind. Main assigns each index once; workers therefore write distinct result elements without resizing the vector. Queue predicates and close are protected by one mutex. Every normal and exceptional path closes the queue and collects workers before local shared state dies. Main prints after collection, so scheduling does not reorder the report. Choose a simpler approach when its narrower contract is enough. Start with a sequential reference and a clear input contract. Parallelize only after measurements show enough work to justify the coordination.

When this system changes, retain a check that exposes the known failure: Let workers push_back into the shared results vector without a lock, or let main return before collecting workers. The first can race on container internals; the second can leave dangling references. Allocate the result slots before starting workers, assign each slot to one input, and keep all shared objects alive through worker completion. Preserve close-and-collect cleanup if any operation fails.

glossary.definition: The inputs, results, and rules that callers and implementations agree to.
A part of a system that performs one kind of work through a defined boundary.
A parameter object initialized from the argument; this vector has independent element storage.
Another name for the caller’s object, with no new copy of that object.
A bit pattern selecting which bit positions an operation should affect.
A fixed group of bits used to store one value within a larger word.
Unsigned arithmetic reduces a result modulo one more than the type’s maximum value.
A rule that must hold before an operation can safely perform its work.
The difference caused when an exact result must be stored as one of the available floating-point values.
An allowed error scaled to the magnitude of the compared values.
Consecutive columns of one row occupy consecutive element positions.
A rule about which addresses are valid starting points for an object type.
A range including its first position but excluding its end position.
An object representing a position that a traversal can examine and advance.
The interval during which a constructed object may be used according to its type’s rules.
Moving responsibility for releasing a resource from one owner to another.
The number of live elements in a container.
The number of elements that fit in currently reserved vector storage without reallocation.
Space that exists but cannot be used for the desired request under an allocator’s rules.
The operation at which a prepared change becomes the visible new state.
An access outside the valid element range of an object.
A program operation for which the C++ standard imposes no behavior requirements.
The registers and other state whose behavior an instruction set promises to software.
The operations and rules a machine exposes to programs.
A named portion of a larger machine register.
Increasing a value’s width by filling the new high bits with zeros.
The address value formed from the components of a machine addressing mode.
A fixed offset included in an address calculation.
The integer result of division after truncation toward zero in this C++ operation.
The part left after multiplying the integer quotient by the divisor.
A rule maintained before every repetition, used to explain the loop’s result.
The order in which a program can execute its operations.
The binary-level agreement for calls, object layout, symbols, and other machine interfaces.
A register whose incoming value a callee must restore when required by the relevant ABI.
Two access paths referring to the same underlying object or storage.
The effects that a valid optimization must preserve under the language’s rules.
A boundary across which code must have different authority to access resources.
Checking that a request satisfies its required shape, range, and permissions before acting on it.
An exception associated with an instruction that could not complete under the current conditions.
The saved execution position used to retry an operation after a recoverable condition is repaired.
Eligible to receive CPU time, though not necessarily executing now.
A permitted change from one named state to another after an event.
The mapping context in which a program interprets its virtual addresses.
The underlying storage reached through a mapping or handle.
A fixed-size block in a virtual address space.
A fixed-size physical-memory block that can back a virtual page.
A record containing mapping information and access-control state for a page.
An exception caused when an access violates the mapping’s permission rules.
A cache of recently used virtual-to-physical translations and related access information.
Removing a cached fact when the authoritative state no longer supports it.
Sharing unchanged backing and making a private copy before a permitted private mutation.
Providing backing for a permitted page when an access first requires it.
The elapsed delay for a particular operation or request.
The amount of data that can be transferred per unit time under stated conditions.
Using nearby locations within a short interval.
Using the same location again before its useful cached state is displaced.
The number of entries in one cache set that can hold competing blocks.
The part of a block’s identity used to distinguish blocks selecting the same set.
An access whose required block is already present and usable at the modeled cache level.
A repeated miss caused by restricted placement relative to the chosen fully associative reference model.
The rule selecting which resident item to remove when space is needed.
A cached block containing changes that must be preserved before the block is discarded.
Misses divided by requests reaching a particular cache level.
Average memory-access time calculated under a stated cost model.
A byte position used to locate data in a file.
A division between logical items imposed by a format above the byte stream.
A process-local handle used to request operations on an open resource.
A successful operation that moves fewer bytes than requested.
Temporarily collecting data so it can be passed onward in useful batches.
Requesting that buffered data move to the next layer defined by the API.
A mapping whose writes affect the shared backing according to the mapping API’s rules.
A mapping whose private modifications do not become shared file changes under its contract.
Kernel-maintained state, such as a file offset, that multiple descriptors may reference.
A process-creation operation that creates a child with defined copies and shared references from its parent.
The executable code and associated user-space state installed in a process.
An operation that replaces the calling process’s program image rather than creating a second process.
Collecting a terminated child’s status so its retained process record can be released.
A result describing how a process terminated; its interpretation depends on the termination category.
End of stream: no more bytes will be delivered under the stream’s contract.
A limit that makes a producer wait or reduce output when a downstream consumer cannot keep up.
An asynchronous process notification with delivery and handling rules defined by the OS.
Permitted for use in an asynchronous signal handler under the applicable API’s rules.
A meaningful input unit such as a word or operator produced during parsing.
A validated description of the operations to perform before those operations are started.
One ordering of steps from activities whose lifetimes overlap.
Multiple activities in progress whose steps may be interleaved or run at the same time.
Waiting for a thread’s completion and establishing the completion relationship needed to use its results.
A division of work into ranges or tasks with explicit coverage and overlap rules.
Conflicting concurrent C++ accesses, at least one a write, without the required atomicity or happens-before ordering.
A result that depends on an undesired ordering of otherwise defined operations.
A pair of atomic ordering operations that can establish visibility of preceding work when the acquire observes the release.
An ordering relation used by C++ to determine whether effects are properly ordered between evaluations.
A region whose operations require coordinated access to shared state.
A synchronization object that permits one cooperating owner at a time.
A waiting mechanism used with a mutex and a predicate over shared state.
A return from waiting that does not itself prove the desired condition is true.
Consume already-accepted work before ending a closed queue or stream.
The rules for stopping new work, waking waiters, finishing or discarding old work, and ending lifetimes.
A state in which participants cannot progress because each waits for conditions the waiting participants must supply.
A cycle of waiting dependencies, such as A waiting for B while B waits for A.
Rules that identify application message boundaries within a sequence of bytes.
An ordered sequence of bytes without a promise that transfer calls preserve message boundaries.
A rule deciding whether new work can enter the system given current resource limits.
The chosen behavior when incoming work exceeds capacity, such as rejection, bounded waiting, or dropping.
A notification that an I/O operation may be able to make progress under the API’s conditions.
A nonblocking result indicating that immediate progress is unavailable without waiting.
Completed work divided by the elapsed measurement interval.
A position in an ordered sample or distribution, interpreted using a stated convention.
Doing reusable work once so later operations require less repeated effort.
How a program’s required work or storage grows with input size.
A time-based bound on whole-system speedup when only a stated fraction of work changes.
A resource or phase that limits the performance of the current workload.
A point where data or actions cross between different levels of trust or authority.
The portion of a buffer that the current operation may treat as meaningful input.
A measure that reduces certain consequences or detects certain failures without necessarily preventing the underlying bug.
Using protections with different coverage so one failed assumption does not remove every defense.
A promise that a failed operation leaves the relevant observable state unchanged.
A guarantee about state surviving the failures specified by a storage protocol, distinct from atomic visibility.
A source unit after preprocessing that the compiler processes under the language’s rules.
Combining compiled definitions and resolving references to build a program or library.
The point at which bounded downstream capacity makes an upstream producer wait or reject work.
A rule spanning several components, such as every accepted input producing exactly one recorded result.
